raw_response.blind_rationale: Blind reading of Frempong, Stadelmann, and Thiam (2025) shows that the study's primary causal analysis investigates an extractive-industry geographic exposure—the count of active and inactive registered commercial mines within 0–50 km and 50–100 km of a household (instrumented with USGS nonfuel mineral deposits)—rather than any legal, regulatory, tenure, tariff, ownership, or administrative service-access rule. While Outcome 1 ('Household gone without clean water' in the past 12 months, binary 0/1, mean 0.36) clearly satisfies Criterion 4 as a household water security/access-continuity measure (note raw sign inversion: 1 = water deprivation, so negative coefficients indicate improved household water security), the headline mining-proximity estimates (Table 2: -0.036, SE 0.005 within 50 km and +0.005, SE 0.002 within 50–100 km; Table 3: -0.027, SE 0.005 for active mines and +0.072, SE 0.117 for inactive mines) fail narrow Criterion 2 (E03) and belong to no SWiM institutional family ('none_nonfit'). In a secondary OLS extension (Figure 1 and Table 4), the authors construct regional average Afrobarometer perception scores for local councillor corruption, tax official corruption, and local government disapproval, and interact councillor corruption with active/inactive mines. Any mining × corruption interaction term (Table 4: printed 0.035, SE 0.004, with conflicting verbal sign descriptions across pp. 597–598 due to stripped minus signs in Wiley's table text layer) is structurally a cross-sector moderation slope ('none_nonfit'). Even if evaluated on the uninstrumented main effect of regional perceived local councillor corruption (+0.106, SE 0.005 in Table 4; +0.10 in Figure 1), the exposure is a broad subjective public-opinion corruption proxy rather than a concrete legal or administrative rule governing WASH service delivery ('borderline_governance_or_proxy', warranting PI scope review under narrow C2 / E03, though if other general perception-based corruption scores were retained in Family A or C, consistency of excluding vs. pooling that main effect should be checked).

raw_response.headline_estimate_summary: Outcome: binary 'Household gone without clean water' in past 12 months (1 = water insecurity/deprivation, 0 = never lacked clean water; mean = 0.36; note raw negative sign = improved water access). N = 142,838 households, adjusted for country & year FEs, respondent age, sex, secondary education, employment, urban dummy, piped water, electricity, clinic, and market (robust SEs; note Wiley PDF table text omits unicode minus signs, verified against prose and Figure 1). (1) Headline 2SLS IV (USGS mineral deposit counts 0–50 km & 50–100 km as IVs; Table 2, Col. 1, PDF p. 9 / p. 594): All active mines within 50 km = -0.036*** (SE = 0.005, p < 0.01; improves water security by 3.6 pp per mine); All active mines within 50–100 km = +0.005*** (SE = 0.002, p < 0.01; worsens water security; KP Wald F = 13.044). (2) Active vs. inactive 2SLS IV within 50 km (Table 3, Col. 1, PDF p. 10 / p. 595): Active mines within 50 km = -0.027*** (SE = 0.005, p < 0.01); Inactive mines within 50 km = +0.072 (SE = 0.117, ns; KP Wald F = 7.716). (3) Local governance OLS LPM estimates (Figure 1, PDF p. 11 / p. 596 & Table 4, Col. 1, PDF p. 12 / p. 597, R2 = 0.069): Regional Corruption (local councillors, 1–4 scale) = +0.106*** (SE = 0.005, p < 0.01; +0.10*** in Fig. 1; worsens water security); Corruption (tax officials) = +0.13*** (Fig. 1); Disapprove local government = +0.05*** (Fig. 1). In Table 4 moderation, Active mines (50 km) * Corruption (local councillors) prints as 0.035*** (SE = 0.004, p < 0.01) and Non-active (50 km) * Corruption prints as 0.040** (SE = 0.013, p < 0.05), with conflicting prose sign interpretations on pp. 597 vs. 598.
raw_response.study_design_and_sample: Repeated cross-sectional georeferenced household survey merged with spatial mining records (2SLS instrumental-variable linear probability models using USGS nonfuel mineral deposits within 0–50 km and 50–100 km as instruments for mining counts, plus uninstrumented OLS LPM governance and moderation models with country and year fixed effects); 28 African countries (Afrobarometer Rounds 3–6, 2005–2015, merged with 435 World Bank Africa-PowerMining sites); unit of analysis is the household/respondent; primary analytic sample N = 142,838 households.
